research_objective: To provide a comprehensive overview of Large Language Models (LLMs), covering architectures, training, evaluation benchmarks, and applications, serving as a foundational reference for the field.
method_or_framework: Systematic literature review and classification of LLMs into seven branches: Pre-Training, Fine-Tuning, Efficient, Inference, Evaluation, Applications, and Challenges.

models_or_population: LLMs with 10B+ parameters (e.g., GPT-3, BLOOM, PaLM, LLaMA, Gopher)
Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) transitioning to LLMs
tasks_or_contexts: Multimodal tasks (e.g., visual reasoning, multimodal CoT)
datasets: Various datasets mentioned in the literature (e.g., GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, BoolQ, DROP, TruthfulQA, MMLU, MATH, BIG-bench)
Datasets for specific domains like medical (CMB), legal (CUAD), and hate speech (Ethos)
metrics: Training stability metrics (e.g., gradient norm, variance)

main_findings.finding: LLMs have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing and generalization, transitioning from PLMs to LLMs by significantly increasing parameters and training data.
Minor changes in architecture and training strategies have a big impact on performance and stability due to the gigantic scale of LLMs.
Layer normalization (Pre-norm) is more common among LLMs for stabilizing training.
Training stability issues like divergence can be mitigated by restarting training from earlier checkpoints, skipping batches, or using embedding layer gradient shrink.
There is an increasing trend towards instruction-tuned and open-source models.

efficiency_or_resource_evidence: Training cost is calculated by multiplying GPU/TPU hourly rate with number of GPUs and training time (e.g., Gopher cost 13.19 Mil, Yuan 1.0 cost 1.32 Mil).
Training parallelism is crucial, with 3D parallelism (data, pipeline, tensor) being most utilized.
Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed are key libraries for scalable distributed training and inference.
limitations: It is challenging to perceive the bigger picture of advances due to the rapid development and plethora of literature.
The survey refers readers interested in smaller pre-trained models to other works.
validity_risks: The survey relies on existing literature which may contain biases or varying standards of reporting.
The 'gigantic scale' of models makes minor changes impactful, potentially introducing instability if not carefully managed.
title: A Comprehensive Overview of Large Language Models

research_objective: To provide a comprehensive review of LLM evaluation methods, focusing on three dimensions: what to evaluate, where to evaluate, and how to evaluate.
method_or_framework: Categorization of evaluation tasks (NLP, reasoning, medical, ethics, etc.), benchmarks, and metrics. It divides benchmarks into general tasks, specific downstream tasks, and multi-modal tasks.

tasks_or_contexts: General NLP tasks (sentiment analysis, classification, NLI, summarization, translation, QA)

main_findings.finding: Evaluation should be treated as an essential discipline to better assist the development of LLMs.
Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench are significant benchmarks that contribute to evaluating chatbot models in realistic scenarios.
HELM provides a comprehensive assessment of LLMs across various aspects like language understanding, generation, coherence, and context sensitivity.
DynaBench supports dynamic benchmark testing, exploring effects of closed-loop integration and model robustness to adversarial attacks.
ToolBench evaluates LLMs' aptitude in understanding complex instructions and utilizing software tools.
SafetyBench reveals substantial security flaws in current LLMs.

limitations: A comprehensive overview capturing the entire gamut of evaluations is still lacking.
The ongoing evolution of LLMs presents novel aspects for evaluation, challenging existing protocols.
validity_risks: The survey relies on existing benchmarks which may not fully capture the dynamic nature of LLM capabilities.
Human-crafted evaluation approaches may not fully reflect emergent abilities.
title: A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models

research_objective: Review recent advances of LLMs, focusing on pre-training, adaptation tuning, utilization, and capacity evaluation.
method_or_framework: Systematic literature review covering four major aspects: pre-training, adaptation tuning, utilization, and capacity evaluation.

models_or_population: Large Language Models (LLMs) including GPT-3, GPT-4, ChatGPT, LLaMA, PaLM
Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) and Statistical/Neural Language Models
datasets: arXiv papers statistics (cumulative numbers of papers containing 'language model' and 'large language model')
Various NLP datasets (mentioned generally, not specific names)
metrics: Hallucination rates (e.g., object hallucination in MLLMs)

main_findings.finding: LLMs display emergent abilities (e.g., in-context learning) that are not present in smaller models when parameter scale exceeds a certain level.
LLMs can serve as general-purpose task solvers, extending task scope from specific tasks to complex real-world tasks.

LLMs are capable of being as general-purpose task solvers but require high overhead for inference, have limitations in modeling long texts, and need special adaptation (e.g., instruction tuning) for specific tasks like text ranking.

LLM-based recommendation models in zero/few-shot settings tend to perform worse than traditional ID-based recommenders, indicating a lack of understanding of personalized user behaviors and domain-specific collaborative semantics.
Current MLLMs often struggle with object hallucination, where the model's responses contain inconsistent content with the image.
LLMs are not directly well suited for existing IR systems due to high inference overhead, limitations in modeling long texts, and the need for special adaptation.

efficiency_or_resource_evidence.detail: LLMs require high overhead for inference, which poses a challenge for deployment in real-world recommender systems.
LLMs have limitations in long context modeling, making it difficult to process huge amounts of user-item interaction data.
Instruction tuning alleviates the gap between LLMs and recommender systems but suffers from high tuning costs.

limitations: LLMs cannot effectively process NLP tasks in low-resource domains (e.g., minor language translation).
LLMs are hard to well address generation tasks about low-resource languages and domains.
LLMs still cannot effectively process the NLP tasks in low-resource domains.
It is still challenging for LLMs to handle complex semantic relations in classic NLP tasks (e.g., nested entity extraction).
LLMs have limited capacities in long context modeling.
LLM-based recommendation models in zero/few-shot settings tend to perform worse than traditional ID-based recommenders.
validity_risks: Hallucination risk in MLLMs (object hallucination).
Hyper-accuracy distortion in LLM-based conversation agents (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT-4).
Potential for LLMs to produce harmful contents in mental well-being support applications.
title: A Survey of Large Language Models

research_objective: Present a comprehensive survey of LLM-based autonomous agents, covering construction, applications, and evaluation strategies.
method_or_framework: Systematic review of LLM-based autonomous agents, proposing a unified framework and summarizing evaluation strategies.

models_or_population: LLM-based autonomous agents (e.g., WebGPT, ReAct, AutoGPT, MetaGPT, Voyager, ChatDev)
Agents in social simulation (e.g., Social Simulacra, Generative Agents, S3)
Agents in education (e.g., Math Agents, CodeHelp, EduChat)
Agents in engineering (e.g., Civil engineering, CS & Software engineering)
tasks_or_contexts: Social science (ideology detection, political speech analysis, economic behavior simulation)
Natural science (mathematical problem solving, scientific research)
Engineering (civil engineering design, software engineering coding/testing)
datasets: Reddit posts (for mental well-being support evaluation)
Various agent-based simulation environments (e.g., virtual towns, social networks)
baselines: Human participants (for comparison in psychology experiments)
metrics: Subjective evaluation (human feedback, alignment with human results)
Objective evaluation (task success rates, consensus answers)
Capability acquisition strategies (fine-tuning vs. no fine-tuning)

main_findings.finding: LLMs have shown potential in attaining human-like intelligence, leading to a surge in research on LLM-based autonomous agents.
Agent architectures can be designed with modules such as Profile, Memory, Planning, and Action to enhance LLM capabilities.
LLM-based agents can help users cope with anxieties, social isolation and depression, but may produce harmful contents.
LLMs are capable of generating results that align with those from studies involving human participants in psychology experiments.
Agents can be evaluated using subjective strategies (e.g., human feedback, crowd-sourcing) and objective strategies (e.g., task success, consensus).

efficiency_or_resource_evidence.detail: Strategies include fine-tuning LLMs or using them without fine-tuning.
Memory operations can be read/write only or include read/write/reflection.
Structures include unified memory (in-context learning) and hybrid memory (short-term and long-term).

limitations: Previous agents assumed simple and heuristic policy functions in isolated environments, diverging from human learning processes.
Agents obtained from previous studies are usually far from replicating human-level decision processes in unconstrained, open-domain settings.
Handcrafting agent profiles is labor-intensive when dealing with a large number of agents.
LLM-generation method may lack precise control over agent profiles.
validity_risks: Agents may produce harmful contents.
Models like ChatGPT and GPT-4 can provide too perfect estimates (hyper-accuracy distortion).
title: A survey on large language model based autonomous agents

research_objective: To provide a comprehensive survey of LLM-based autonomous agents, covering their construction (architecture and capability acquisition), applications, and evaluation strategies.
method_or_framework: Taxonomy and Unified Framework. The authors propose a unified agent framework comprising a profiling module, a memory module, a planning module, and an action module (Fig. 2). They categorize agent capability acquisition into fine-tuning methods and non-fine-tuning methods (e.g., mechanism engineering).

models_or_population: LLM-based autonomous agents (e.g., WebGPT, Voyager, ToolBench, AgentSims, AutoGPT, AgentGPT, ChatDev, RecAgent, GITM, MIND2WEB, CO-LLM, TALM, HuggingGPT, DEPS, RoCo, PREFER, Social Simulacra, Generative Agents, AgentSims, SocialAI School, S3, CGMI, Chatlaw, Agentbench, Webarena, Bolaa, Gentopia, Emotionbench, Agentbench, Webarena, etc.)
tasks_or_contexts: Social Science (Psychology, Political Science, Social Simulation, Research Assistant)
Engineering (Civil Engineering, Computer Science, Aerospace, Jurisprudence, Industrial Automation, Robotics & Embodied AI)
baselines: Not explicitly detailed as baselines in the survey text, but various agent models are compared and categorized.
metrics: Objective Evaluation (Evaluation Metric, Evaluation Protocol, Evaluation Benchmark)

main_findings.finding: LLMs possess comprehensive internal world knowledge, enabling informed actions without specific domain training, unlike traditional RL agents.
A unified framework for agent architecture design is proposed, encompassing profiling, memory, planning, and action modules.
Agent capability acquisition strategies include fine-tuning (adjusting model parameters) and non-fine-tuning (prompt engineering, mechanism engineering).
LLM-based agents can help users cope with anxieties, social isolation, and depression, but may produce harmful contents.
LLM-based agents can simulate social phenomena (e.g., harmful information propagation) and human daily life in virtual environments.
Evaluation strategies for LLM-based agents include subjective (human annotation, Turing test) and objective (metrics, protocols, benchmarks) approaches.

limitations: Previous studies often assume agents act based on simple heuristic policies in isolated environments, diverging from human learning processes.
Non-fine-tuning methods cannot incorporate too much task information due to LLM input context window limitations.
Designing optimal prompts and mechanisms is challenging due to the large search space.
validity_risks: Hallucination issue prevalent in LLMs (mitigated by self-attention mechanism in some models).
Hyper-accuracy distortion may influence downstream applications.
title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents

research_objective: To provide a comprehensive survey on LLM-based agents, tracing the concept of agents, presenting a general framework (brain, perception, action), exploring applications (single-agent, multi-agent, human-agent cooperation), and discussing agent societies, open problems, and risks.
method_or_framework: General Framework and Categorization. The authors present a general framework for LLM-based agents comprising three main components: brain, perception, and action. They categorize applications into single-agent, multi-agent, and human-agent cooperation scenarios, and explore agent societies.

tasks_or_contexts: Agent society simulation (Text-based, Virtual Sandbox, Physical environments)
datasets: Not explicitly detailed in the text provided.
baselines: Not explicitly detailed as baselines in the survey text.
metrics: Sociability (Language communication proficiency, Cooperation and negotiation, Role-playing capability)

main_findings.finding: LLMs are regarded as potential sparks for AGI and suitable foundations for building general AI agents.
A general framework for LLM-based agents is proposed, comprising brain, perception, and action.
Evaluation of sociability includes language communication proficiency, cooperation and negotiation abilities, and role-playing capability.
LLMs are susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can lead to erroneous answers or destructive actions.
Potential risks include misuse (manipulating public opinion, cybersecurity threats), unemployment, and threats to human well-being.

limitations: Previous studies have focused on enhancing specific capabilities or performance on particular tasks, overlooking the development of inherent general abilities like knowledge memorization, long-term planning, and efficient interaction.
The question of how LLMs can efficiently plan and utilize action abilities remains unresolved.
Ensuring agents are harmless and adhere to ethical guidelines is paramount.
validity_risks: Adversarial robustness: LLMs are susceptible to adversarial attacks (dataset poisoning, backdoor attacks, prompt-specific attacks).
Misuse: Agents can be exploited for malicious purposes.
Unemployment: Agents may replace human jobs.
Threat to human well-being: Humans may struggle to control advanced agents.
title: The Rise and Potential of Large Language Model Based Agents: A Survey

research_objective: To provide a comprehensive review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms, covering the progression from Naive RAG to Advanced and Modular RAG, and to introduce up-to-date evaluation frameworks and benchmarks.
method_or_framework: A survey reviewing the tripartite foundation of RAG frameworks: Retrieval, Generation, and Augmentation. It categorizes RAG into three stages: Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG.

models_or_population: Various RAG systems and components (e.g., embedding models like AngIE, Voyage, BGE; reranking models like Cohere, bge-raranker-large; LLMs like GPT)
Embedding models evaluated on MTEB leaderboard (8 tasks, 58 datasets) and C-MTEB (6 tasks, 35 datasets)
tasks_or_contexts: Question Answering (QA) including single-hop/multi-hop, multiple-choice, domain-specific, and long-form scenarios
Information Extraction (IE), dialogue generation, code search
datasets: Various downstream tasks summarized in Table II (26 tasks, nearly 50 datasets)
metrics: EM (Exact Match) and F1 scores for QA
Embedding model performance metrics on MTEB/C-MTEB

main_findings.finding: RAG effectively reduces hallucination and enhances accuracy for knowledge-intensive tasks by incorporating external knowledge.
Naive RAG faces challenges in retrieval precision/recall, generation hallucination, and augmentation disjointedness.

Advanced RAG and Modular RAG offer greater flexibility through pre-retrieval optimization (e.g., query rewriting, HyDE, Step-back Prompting) and post-retrieval processes (e.g., reranking, context compression).
Embedding models are task-specific; no single model fits all use cases, though multi-task instruct tuning improves generalization.
Context selection/compression is crucial to avoid the 'Lost in the middle' problem and reduce noise from excessive retrieved documents.
Iterative, Recursive, and Adaptive retrieval processes can enhance robustness by offering additional contextual references.

limitations: RAG development faces challenges in retrieval precision/recall, generation hallucination, and augmentation disjointedness.
No one-size-fits-all embedding model exists.
Excessive context can introduce noise and cause the 'Lost in the middle' problem.
title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey

research_objective: To address three pivotal questions regarding tool-augmented LLMs: (1) How effective are current LLMs in utilizing tools? (2) How can we enhance LLMs' ability to utilize tools? (3) What obstacles need to be overcome to leverage tools?
method_or_framework: API-Bank is a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 73 real-world APIs and 314 tool-use dialogues. It defines three levels of API usage abilities: Call, Retrieval+Call, and Plan+Retrieve+Call. It also introduces a Multi-agent method for automated data generation.

datasets: API-Bank Evaluation Set (314 dialogues, 753 API calls)
API-Bank Training Set (1,888 dialogues, 4,149 API calls, 2,138 APIs, 1,000 domains)
baselines: Alpaca-7B, ChatGLM-6B, GPT-3 Davinci, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4
metrics: Error type distribution (No API Call, API Hallucination, Invalid Input Parameters, etc.)

main_findings.finding: Even smaller models (Alpaca-7B, ChatGLM-6B) possess some API call accuracy (~20%), but proficiency in API retrieval and planning is negligible.
GPT-3 Davinci exhibits almost no capability in API usage, indicating API usage might not be an inherent feature of LLMs.
GPT-3.5 exhibits improved tool utilization compared to GPT-3, while GPT-4 excels in planning.
Lynx (fine-tuned on API-Bank) surpasses Alpaca-7B by more than 26 points in API Call correctness and approaches GPT-3.5's effectiveness.
The primary error for Alpaca is 'No API Call' (36.77%), while GPT-4's primary error is 'Failed API Retrieval' (67.86%).

limitations: API-Bank focuses solely on English.
Only fine-tuned Lynx-7B was explored; larger-scale models were not tested.
Evaluation set is manually constructed, making it more realistic but potentially less diverse than LLM-generated benchmarks.
title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs

research_objective: To provide a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of LLM agent evaluation, introducing a two-dimensional taxonomy (Evaluation Objectives and Evaluation Process) and highlighting enterprise-specific challenges.
method_or_framework: Taxonomy-based survey organizing existing work along (1) evaluation objectives (what to evaluate) and (2) evaluation process (how to evaluate).

tasks_or_contexts: Agent Capabilities (tool use, planning, memory, multi-agent collaboration)
metrics: Success Rate (SR), F1-score, Pass@k, Progress Rate, Execution Accuracy
Latency (TTFT, End-to-End Request Latency), Token Usage, Cost
Invocation Accuracy, Tool Selection Accuracy, Retrieval Accuracy (MRR, NDCG), Parameter name F1 score
Reasoning Quality, Accuracy, Fine-Grained Progress Rate, Self Consistency, Plan Quality
Information Sharing Effectiveness, Adaptive Role Switching
Accuracy, Task Success Rate Under Perturbation
Coverage, Violation Rate, Transparency, Ethics, Morality
Adversarial Robustness, Prompt Injection Resistance, Harmfulness, Bias Detection

main_findings.finding: Evaluating LLM agents is more complex than evaluating LLMs due to the need to assess behavior, capabilities, reliability, and safety in dynamic environments.
A two-dimensional taxonomy is proposed: Evaluation Objectives (Agent Behavior, Capabilities, Reliability, Safety) and Evaluation Process (Interaction Mode, Data, Metrics, Tooling).

Tool use evaluation involves answering whether to invoke a tool, selecting the correct tool, and identifying correct parameters. Metrics include Invocation Accuracy, Tool Selection Accuracy, Retrieval Accuracy (MRR, NDCG), and Parameter name F1 score.
Robustness evaluation involves stress-testing with perturbed inputs (paraphrased instructions, irrelevant context, linguistic variations) and measuring performance degradation.
Reliability assessment is nontrivial due to inherent stochasticity; measuring consistency requires executing the same task multiple times (e.g., pass^k metric).
Enterprise-specific challenges include role-based access control, reliability guarantees, dynamic and long-horizon interactions, and compliance requirements.
Evaluation methods include code-based methods (deterministic, objective) and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches (handling subjective responses).

efficiency_or_resource_evidence.evidence: Cost is estimated based on the number of input and output tokens, correlating with usage-based pricing.
Running multiple trials per input for consistency evaluation introduces significant computational overhead.

limitations: Current benchmarks often focus on short episodes or single interactions, lacking the ability to capture phenomena such as performance drift or cumulative effects over time.
Standard, short-term evaluations cannot fully address the complexity of real-world enterprise agents operating continuously over extended periods.
Code-based methods are typically inflexible and struggle with evaluating open-ended or qualitative responses.
LLM-as-a-Judge introduces complexity due to the need for multiple AI agents interacting depending on their roles.
validity_risks: Hallucinated parameter values in tool calls may be missed by AST-based evaluations.
LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations can be subjective and complex to implement correctly.
Enterprise-specific challenges like role-based access are often overlooked in current research.
title: Evaluation and Benchmarking of LLM Agents: A Survey

research_objective: To systematically investigate and comprehensively review tool-learning agents, covering definitions, architectures, retrieval methods, planning strategies, and benchmarks.
method_or_framework: Review of tool-learning agents, categorized by tool retrieval (training-based vs. non-training-based) and planning methods (internal vs. external).

tasks_or_contexts: Tool Invocation (whether to use a tool)
datasets: Not explicitly listed as a primary dataset, but references various benchmarks like Gorilla, ToolBench, API-Bank.
metrics: Not explicitly detailed in the provided text, but mentions evaluation dimensions and assessment.

main_findings.finding: Tool learning tasks are defined by the 'Three Ws': Whether (invocation), Which (retrieval), and How (usage).
Tool retrieval is categorized into training-based and non-training-based methods.
Tool planning methods are organized based on whether they rely on the model's inherent reasoning capabilities or utilize external reasoning tools (symbolic planners like PDDL).
Multi-modal tools are discussed to address ambiguity in understanding user intentions and to handle visual or audio-grounded instructions.
Applications include data science (databases, finance), software engineering (code generation, error analysis), and robotics (simulation-based and real-time control).

limitations: Text-based tool learning cannot clearly understand user intentions, limiting the ability to address multimodal problems.
The lack of tool planning, such as selecting tools for sub-tasks and ordering tools, makes it difficult to invoke tools effectively in multitasking scenarios.
Most toolsets provide methods to verify parameter accuracy and return statuses, but tool documentation can become outdated.
validity_risks: Ambiguity in understanding user intentions due to text-based perception.
Tool documentation may become outdated as invocation methods and data sources change.
title: LLM-Based Agents for Tool Learning: A Survey

research_objective: Review the landscape of utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) in agent-based modeling and simulation, analyzing challenges in environment perception, human alignment, action generation, and evaluation.
method_or_framework: Systematic analysis of agent capabilities (autonomy, social ability, reactivity, proactiveness) and categorization of works into cyber, physical, social, and hybrid domains.

datasets: Representative papers listed in Table 1 (e.g., SimReddit, COLA, MAD, MetaGPT)
baselines: Predefined rules and symbolic equations (e.g., cellular automata, social force model)
metrics: SOTA performance on stance detection tasks (reported for COLA)
Performance comparison in cooperative tasks (reported for various frameworks)

main_findings.finding: LLM agents can serve as a new paradigm for simulation with human-level intelligence, capable of autonomous action, adaptive planning, and interaction.
LLM agents can exhibit human-like social phenomena such as conformity and the Wisdom of Crowds effect.
LLM agents can replicate social network formation dynamics influenced by triadic closure and homophily.
LLM agents can achieve SOTA performance on specific tasks like stance detection (COLA).
LLM agents can simulate complex behaviors in software development (ChatDev) and economic systems.

limitations: No survey systematically summarizes relevant works, discusses unresolved issues, and provides research directions (as of the paper's publication).
Agents cannot make perfectly rational choices due to limitations of knowledge and computational capacity (Simon, 1997).
validity_risks: Simulation fidelity depends on the quality of the LLM and the agent design.
Potential for hallucinations or incorrect reasoning in complex simulations.
title: Large language models empowered agent-based modeling and simulation: a survey and perspectives

research_objective: Advocate for the development of 'Artificial Intelligence Structured Clinical Examinations' (AI-SCE) to evaluate LLM agents in clinical settings, moving beyond standardized benchmarks.
method_or_framework: Proposes a framework for high-fidelity simulation of clinical settings (patient-physician interactions, hospital processes) using agent-based modeling (ABM), drawing parallels to autonomous vehicle testing.

datasets: Real-world electronic health records (e.g., MIMIC-IV, UCSF Information Commons)
baselines: Standardized clinical NLP benchmarks (e.g., MedQA, MedNLI)
metrics: Diagnostic accuracy (referenced for AMIE and GPT-4)

main_findings.finding: Current benchmarks (MedQA, MedNLI) are insufficient for capturing the full range of capabilities demonstrated by clinical LLM agents.
LLM agents can be modeled in high-fidelity simulations of clinical settings to assess their impact on clinical workflows.
Agent-based modeling can be used to evaluate how an LLM agent interacts with users, employs tools, and identifies points of failure.

limitations: Requires robust clinical guidelines to define success in interactions.
Requires high-quality, de-identified data for realistic simulations.
validity_risks: Data privacy concerns when using real-world EHRs.
Potential for bias in simulated patient behaviors if derived from limited datasets.
title: Evaluating large language models as agents in the clinic
